claims.text: Contrastive methods for EBM training push down energy on training samples and pull up energy on contrastive samples, but only affect the energy surface where contrastive samples are placed.
claims.quote: Contrastive methods (top right) push down on the energy of training samples (blue dots) and pulls up on the energies of suitably-placed contrastive samples (green dots).

claims.text: Regularized methods minimize the volume of low-energy regions while pushing down energy on training samples, causing low-energy regions to wrap around data-dense areas.
claims.quote: regularized methods (bottom right) push down on the energy of training samples and use a regularizer term that minimizes the volume of low-energy regions.

claims.text: Contrastive methods require the number of contrastive samples to grow exponentially with the dimensionality of y space in high dimensions.
claims.quote: a disadvantage of contrastive methods is that the number of contrastive samples necessary to make an energy surface adopt a good shape may grow exponentially with the dimension of y space.

claims.text: Distance-dependent hinge loss makes energy grow at least quadratically with distance from the data manifold.
claims.quote: This makes the energy grow at least quadratically with the distance to the data manifold.

claims.text: Contrastive methods include Siamese networks, DrLIM, PIRL, MoCO, SimCLR, CPT, and other recent approaches with pairs where x is a distorted version of y.
claims.quote: Contrastive methods are very popular, particularly for Siamese network architectures trained with pairs where x is a distorted or corrupted version of y and ˆy another random (or suitably chosen) training sample. This includes such methods as the original Siamese net, as well as more recent methods including DrLIM, PIRL, MoCO, SimCLR, CPT, and others.

claims.text: Generative Adversarial Networks can be seen as contrastive methods where contrastive samples are produced by a trainable generator network.
claims.quote: Generative Adversarial Networks can also be seen as contrastive methods in which the ˆy are produced by the trainable generator network.

claims.text: Denoising Auto-Encoders and Masked Auto-Encoders are examples of contrastive training where contrastive samples are generated by corrupting clean data.
claims.quote: Denoising Auto-Encoders and their special case, Masked Auto-Encoders, are also examples of contrastive training methods in which the ˆy is generated by corrupting the clean y.

claims.text: The main problems with contrastive methods are designing a scheme to generate suitable contrastive samples and the exponential growth requirement in high dimensions.
claims.quote: First, one has to design a scheme to generate or pick suitable ˆy. Second, when y is in a high-dimensional space, and if the EBM is flexible, it may require a very large number of contrastive samples to ensure that the energy is higher in all dimensions unoccupied by the local data distribution.

claims.text: Regularized methods are more promising than contrastive methods because they avoid the curse of dimensionality by minimizing the volume of low-energy regions.
claims.quote: Regularized methods for EBM training are much more promising in the long run than contrastive methods because they can eschew the curse of dimensionality that plagues contrastive methods.

claims.text: Examples of non-contrastive regularized methods include sparse modeling, sparse auto-encoders, and VAE.
claims.quote: Examples include sparse modeling, sparse auto-encoders, and auto-encoders with noisy latent variables, such as VAE.

claims.text: Contrastive and regularized methods can be used simultaneously on the same model.
claims.quote: It is important to note that contrastive and regularized methods are not incompatible with each other, and can be used simultaneously on the same model.

claims.text: In latent-variable generative architectures, restricting information capacity of z restricts the volume of y space that can take low energy.
claims.quote: In the latent-variable generative architecture, restricting the information capacity of z will restrict the volume of y space that can take low energy.

claims.text: In auto-encoder architectures, restricting information capacity of sy restricts the volume of y space that can be reconstructed with low energy.
claims.quote: Similarly, in the auto-encoder architecture, restricting the information capacity of sy will restrict the volume of y space that can be reconstructed with low energy.

claims.text: In Joint Embedding Architecture, maximizing information that sx and sy contain about x and y minimizes the volume of y space that can take low energy.
claims.quote: Lastly, in the Joint Embedding Architecture, Maximizing the information that sx contains about x and sy contains about y will minimize the volume of y space that can take low energy.

claims.text: JEPA combines Joint Embedding Architecture and Latent-Variable Generative Architecture and is non-generative, predicting the representation of y rather than y itself.
claims.quote: In the following, we will focus on an architecture for SSL the Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) which can seen as a combination of the Joint Embedding Architecture and the Latent-Variable Generative Architecture. The JEPA is non-generative in that it does not actually predict y, but predicts the representation of y, sy from that of x, sx.

claims.text: The energy in JEPA is the prediction error between the predicted representation and actual representation in representation space.
claims.quote: The energy is simply the prediction error in representation space: Ew(x, y, z) = D(sy, Pred(sx, z))

claims.text: JEPA's main advantage is that it performs predictions in representation space, avoiding the need to predict every detail of y.
claims.quote: The main advantage of JEPA is that it performs predictions in representation space, eschewing the need to predict every detail of y.

claims.text: JEPA can represent multi-modality through encoder invariance properties that map multiple y values to the same sy.
claims.quote: The encoder function sy = Enc(y) may have invariance properties. If all the y's in a set map to the same value of sy, all those y's will have identical energies.

claims.text: JEPA can represent multi-modality through a latent variable z that captures information necessary to predict sy not present in sx.
claims.quote: The predictor may use a latent variable z to capture the information necessary to predict sy that is not present in sx.

claims.text: JEPA can be trained with non-contrastive methods using four criteria: maximize information in sx, maximize information in sy, make sy predictable from sx, and minimize information in z.
claims.quote: The basic principle of such training is that (1) sx should be maximally informative about x; (2) sy should be maximally informative about y; (3) sy should be easily predictable from sx; and (4) z should have minimal information content.

claims.text: Criteria 1 and 2 in JEPA training prevent energy surface collapse by ensuring sx and sy carry maximum information about their inputs.
claims.quote: Criteria 1 and 2 prevent the energy surface from becoming flat by informational collapse. They ensure that sx and sy carry as much information as possible about their inputs.

claims.text: Criterion 3 in JEPA training is enforced by the energy term and ensures y is predictable from x in representation space.
claims.quote: Criterion 3 is enforced by the energy term D(sy, ˜sy) and ensures that y is predictable from x in representation space.

claims.text: Criterion 4 prevents informational collapse by forcing the model to predict sy with minimal help from the latent variable.
claims.quote: Criterion 4 prevents the system from falling victim to another type of informational collapse by forcing the model to predict sy with as little help from the latent as possible.

claims.text: If z has the same dimension as sy, the predictor could ignore sx and copy z to produce zero energy, creating a collapsed energy surface.
claims.quote: Imagine that z has the same dimension as sy. Assume that the predictor is a parameterized function (e.g. a neural net) that can choose to ignore sx and to simply copy z on its output ˜sy = z. For any sy it is possible to set ˇz = sy, which would make the energy D(sy, ˜sy) zero.

claims.text: Information content of latent variable z can be minimized by making it discrete, low-dimensional, sparse, or noisy.
claims.quote: By making z discrete, low-dimensional, sparse, or noisy, among other methods.

claims.text: When z is discrete with K values, there can only be K possible values of sy with zero energy in a K-well energy landscape.
claims.quote: Hence, these can be the only values of sy with zero energy, and there are only K of them.

claims.text: When z is a low-dimensional vector, the set of possible predictions forms at most a d-dimensional manifold in representation space.
claims.quote: Then, assuming that Pred(sx, z) is a smooth function of z, the set of possible predictions will be at most a d-dimensional manifold in the space of sy.

claims.text: L1 regularization on z drives z to sparsity and causes low-energy regions to be approximated by unions of low-dimensional manifolds.
claims.quote: This will drive ˇz to be sparse. As with classical sparse coding, this will cause the region of low energy to be approximated by a union of low-dimensional manifolds

claims.text: Four classes of methods minimize information content of latent variables: discretization/quantification, dimensionality/rank minimization, sparsification, and fuzzyfication.
claims.quote: we can mention four classes of methods: discretization/quantification (e.g. as in VQ-VAE (Walker et al., 2021), dimensionality/rank minimization (e.g. as in Implicit Rank-Minimizing AE (Jing et al., 2020), sparsification (as in linear sparse modeling (Olshausen and Field, 1996), LISTA (Gregor and LeCun, 2010b), and non-linear sparse modeling (Evtimova and LeCun, 2022)), and fuzzyfication (as in noisy AE (Doi et al., 2007), VAE (Kingma and Welling, 2013), and variants used in control problems (Henaff et al., 2019)).

claims.text: JEPA is preferable to generative models because predicting every pixel value in video frames is impossible, but JEPA can predict abstract representations.
claims.quote: The ability of the JEPA to predict in representation space makes it considerably preferable to generative models that directly produce a prediction of y. In a video prediction scenario, it is essentially impossible to predict every pixel value of every future frame.

claims.text: VICReg and Barlow Twins are examples of non-contrastive criteria for JEPA training.
claims.quote: Examples of such non-contrastive criteria for JEPA training include VICReg and Barlow Twins.
